title: Sudden and gradual
hookLine: Chinul: awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually

cards: A frozen pond in winter. One glance tells you the whole thing is water. Not partly.
All of it. And yet you can't drink it, swim in it, or wash your hands in it. Knowing it's water doesn't melt it.
That takes days of sun. A Korean monk named Chinul used that pond to answer an argument that had run through Chan for a long time, the one from the wall where two verses were written.

teach.b: Some days back, two verses went up on a monastery wall. One said the mind is a mirror that must be wiped clean, again and again. Huineng's answer said there is no mirror for dust to land on.
People came to sum up the two sides as gradual and sudden: is awakening built up step by step, or seen all at once? Chinul was a Korean monk of the Goryeo kingdom who trained and taught in Korea.
In a short work called Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, he says: both, in order.
First you awaken suddenly. You see, all at once, that your own mind is already the Buddha-nature, the way you see that ice is water. Then you cultivate gradually.

teach.h: A NEWBORN STILL HAS TO GROW.
teach.b: Old habits are still frozen in place, and they take time and steady practice to thaw. He gives another picture.

A newborn baby, Chinul writes, has all the senses and limbs of a grown person, nothing missing, but it takes years before that strength is fully grown. Awakening is like being born. Practice is like growing up.
Insight tends to arrive in a flash: in a conversation, on a walk, at a funeral. It's tempting to think the flash is the finish.
Chinul says the flash is the start.
The seeing is real, and the thaw still has to happen. Korean Seon, Korea's Chan, still looks back to Chinul as one of its great teachers.

how: In Korean Seon, Chinul's teaching of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation is studied in monasteries, and his short works, such as Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, are read by monks and lay practitioners.

o: the awakened mind already in you, still to thaw
the personal character of the historical Buddha
a nature you earn after many lifetimes of merit

games.q: sudden and gradual: tap the pairs.
p: nothing missing, still has to grow

s: Chinul taught that once you awaken, practice is finished
he taught the reverse: awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually.
Chinul compared awakening to seeing that a frozen pond is water
knowing it's water doesn't melt it. that takes time and warmth.
Chinul simply picked the sudden side of the old argument
he joined the two, in order: first sudden, then gradual.

games.q: you're Chinul. one side says awakening is sudden; the other says it's gradual. how do you answer?
o: it's sudden, so drop the practice.
it's gradual, so the flash is an illusion.
both: awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually.
games.why: Chinul puts them in order: the seeing comes at once, the habits thaw slowly, like ice known to be water.

practice: Bring back one thing you once saw clearly, in a flash, about yourself, someone you love, or how you want to live.
Gently ask where the ice is still frozen, where the old habit still runs, and without scolding it, sit beside it like sun on a pond.

wordCard.voice: Buddha-nature. The true mind Chinul says you see all at once, then thaw slowly through steady practice.

carryVoice: Your line: sudden, then slowly. The ice is water already; the thaw takes its time. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chinul, Secrets on Cultivating the Mind (Susim gyeol)
